cards.front: Recall a key point about Kaiser Wilhelm and Germany
cards.back: Kaiser Wilhelm II became German Emperor (Kaiser) in June 1888 aged 29, following the death of his father Frederick III who had ruled for only 99 days. Wilhelm would reign until his abdication in November 1918.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Kaiser Wilhelm and Germany
cards.back: Germany was a federal state with 25 states in 1871 (27 after 1912), each retaining its own ruler, government and laws. The Prussian King was automatically the German Kaiser.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Kaiser Wilhelm and Germany
cards.back: Prussia was the largest and most powerful state in Germany. It covered 60% of German territory and contained 65% of the population. The King of Prussia was always the Kaiser.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Kaiser Wilhelm and Germany
cards.back: Weltpolitik ("world policy") was Wilhelm II's aggressive foreign policy aiming to make Germany a major world power with colonies, a large navy, and international influence. It replaced Bismarck's Realpolitik ("practical politics") which had focused on maintaining peace and stability in Europe.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Kaiser Wilhelm and Germany
cards.back: Admiral von Tirpitz and Wilhelm II pushed through a series of Navy Laws (1898, 1900, 1906, 1908, 1912) to build a fleet capable of challenging the Royal Navy. The aim was to make Germany a world power and force Britain to respect German interests.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Kaiser Wilhelm and Germany
cards.back: The Social Democratic Party (SPD) was the main opposition to the Kaiser's regime. By 1912, the SPD was the largest party in the Reichstag with 110 seats (34.8% of the vote), yet the government continued to ignore its demands for reform.

cards.front: Recall a key point about Kaiser Wilhelm and Germany
cards.back: Bismarck introduced social welfare legislation in the 1880s specifically to undermine support for the SPD. However, the measures were too limited to satisfy workers and the SPD continued to grow. By 1912, despite 30 years of social welfare, the SPD was the largest party in the Reichstag.

cards.front: What should you know about history exam tips — kaiser wilhelm and germany?
cards.back: 1. For Kaiser Wilhelm and Germany, include specific factual detail: dates, names, events and statistics where relevant 2. For source questions, analyse provenance (who, when, why, audience) before using the content 3. In evaluation questions, discuss multiple factors and weigh their relative significance 4. Always link back to the question focus — don't just narrate what happened with Kaiser Wilhelm and Germany 5. Use phrases like 'the most significant factor was... because...' to show analytical judgement
Head of state, commander-in-chief (e.g. Appointed/dismissed the Chancellor, could dissolve the Reichstag, controlled foreign policy and the armed forces)
Head of government (e.g. Responsible only to the Kaiser, not the Reichstag; could ignore the Reichstag entirely)
Upper house (Federal Council) (e.g. 58 members from state governments; could veto legislation; Prussia had 17 of 58 votes (effective veto))
Lower house (elected parliament) (e.g. Elected by all men over 25; could approve or reject laws and set the budget; but the Kaiser could dissolve it at any time)

cards.front: What does Universal male suffrage (all men over 25 could vote) mean?
cards.back: Secret ballot introduced but influence of landlords remained

cards.front: What does Reichstag elected every 3 years (5 years from 1888) mean?
cards.back: Kaiser could dissolve the Reichstag at will

cards.front: What does Reichstag had to approve laws and budgets mean?
cards.back: Bundesrat (dominated by Prussia) could veto any law
